options: The variable with the highest variance
The linear combination of original variables capturing the most variance
The first variable listed in the dataset
The average of all standardised variables
questions.explanation: PC1 is the linear combination of the original variables that captures the maximum variance. It is a new synthetic variable, not one of the original variables.

questions.text: PCA requires that input variables are:
questions.explanation: PCA is based on variance and covariance — concepts only meaningful for numeric variables. Variables must be scaled so that high-variance variables do not dominate the PCs regardless of their meaning.

questions.text: Principal components are correlated with each other.
questions.explanation: PCs are orthogonal (perpendicular) to each other by construction. This means they are uncorrelated — each captures variance not explained by any previous component. Absence of multicollinearity among PCs is one of their main advantages.

questions.text: The scree plot shows 40% variance explained by PC1, 25% by PC2, and 15% by PC3. How many PCs would you retain using the '80% total variance' rule?
questions.explanation: Cumulative variance: PC1 = 40%, PC1+PC2 = 65%, PC1+PC2+PC3 = 80%. So 3 PCs are needed to explain 80% of the total variance.

questions.text: In a loadings plot, PC1 has large positive loadings on num_claims and claim_amount, and a large negative loading on customer_rating. This suggests PC1 represents:
options: Policy tenure (how long the policyholder has been enrolled)
questions.explanation: High positive loadings on claim-related variables and a negative loading on customer_rating together define a dimension where moving in the positive PC1 direction means more claims and lower satisfaction — a 'high utilisation / dissatisfied' segment.
